description: The primary UK anti-bribery statute. Creates four offences: Section 1 (active bribery — bribing another person), Section 2 (passive bribery — being bribed), Section 6 (bribery of a foreign public official), Section 7 (corporate failure to prevent bribery). Section 7 has near-unlimited territorial reach — applies to any commercial organisation with a UK nexus. Maximum penalties: 10 years imprisonment (individuals), unlimited fines (corporates). Enforced by the Serious Fraud Office (SFO).

US federal statute prohibiting bribery of foreign public officials. Two sets of provisions: (1) Anti-bribery provisions (15 USC 78dd-1/2/3) — prohibit offering, paying, promising anything of value to a foreign official to obtain/retain business; (2) Accounting provisions (15 USC 78m) — require issuers to maintain accurate books and records and adequate internal controls. Extraterritorial scope: applies to US issuers, US persons, and any act in US territory. Jointly enforced by DOJ (criminal) and SEC (civil/regulatory).

Convention on Combating Bribery of Foreign Public Officials in International Business Transactions. Signed 1997, in force 1999. 44 signatory countries including all OECD members. Requires signatories to criminalise bribery of foreign public officials. Monitored by the OECD Working Group on Bribery through Phase 1-4 country evaluations. Provides the international framework underpinning the FCPA, UKBA, and equivalent national laws.

The broadest international anti-corruption treaty. In force 2005. 189 state parties. Covers: bribery (domestic and foreign officials), embezzlement, trading in influence, money laundering, obstruction of justice, illicit enrichment, private sector corruption. Requires asset recovery, international cooperation, and preventive measures. Monitored by the Implementation Review Mechanism (IRM) under UNODC. UNCAC links bribery directly to money laundering as predicate offence.

European Commission proposal (COM(2023)234) for a directive on combating corruption. Would harmonise criminal law definitions and sanctions across EU member states for: active/passive bribery, trading in influence, abuse of functions, embezzlement, obstruction of justice. Minimum criminal sanctions: 5 years imprisonment. Replaces fragmented national approaches. References UNCAC and GRECO recommendations. Involves EPPO for trans-border cases. Status: legislative procedure ongoing (2024-2025).

International standard specifying requirements for an anti-bribery management system. Published 2016, updated 2021. Aligns with ISO management system structure. Key requirements: leadership commitment, anti-bribery policy, risk assessment, due diligence on business associates, financial controls, reporting mechanisms, training, monitoring, and continuous improvement. Certification by accredited body provides prima facie evidence of adequate procedures for UKBA Section 7 defence purposes.

canonical_name: UK Bribery Act s.1 — Active Bribery (Bribing Another Person)
description: UKBA 2010 Section 1: A person is guilty of bribery if they offer, promise, or give a financial or other advantage to another person intending to induce improper performance of a function or reward it. No requirement that the bribe be paid to a public official — covers private sector bribery. Applies to conduct by UK nationals or residents, or where any act/omission occurs in the UK. Maximum: 10 years imprisonment.

canonical_name: UK Bribery Act s.2 — Passive Bribery (Being Bribed)
description: UKBA 2010 Section 2: A person is guilty of being bribed if they request, agree to receive, or accept a financial or other advantage intending that a relevant function be performed improperly, or as a reward for improper performance. Covers both public and private sector recipients. Maximum: 10 years imprisonment. Widely interpreted: 'improper performance' covers breach of an expectation of good faith, impartiality, or trust.

canonical_name: UK Bribery Act s.6 — Bribery of Foreign Public Officials
description: UKBA 2010 Section 6: A person commits an offence if they offer/promise/give a financial or other advantage to a foreign public official (FPO) intending to influence the FPO in their capacity as FPO, to obtain or retain business or a business advantage. Unlike s.1, no need to prove 'improper performance' — intent to influence is sufficient. Facilitation payments are NOT exempt (unlike FCPA). Critical for international business in high-risk jurisdictions.

canonical_name: UK Bribery Act s.7 — Corporate Failure to Prevent Bribery
description: UKBA 2010 Section 7: A commercial organisation is guilty of an offence if a person associated with it bribes another person intending to obtain/retain business or a business advantage for the organisation. This is a strict liability offence — no intent required. Single defence: the organisation had in place 'adequate procedures' designed to prevent bribery. 'Associated persons' include employees, agents, subsidiaries, and joint venture partners. Near-unlimited territorial reach: applies to any UK-connected commercial organisation regardless of where bribery occurred.

FCPA anti-bribery provisions prohibit: issuers (78dd-1), domestic concerns (78dd-2), and any person in US territory (78dd-3) from corruptly offering/paying/promising anything of value to a foreign official to influence official acts or decisions and obtain/retain business. Key elements: (1) payment/offer/promise; (2) to a foreign official; (3) corrupt intent; (4) for business purpose. Affirmative defences: (a) lawful under written laws of the foreign country; (b) bona fide promotional expenses. Facilitation payments are a narrow FCPA exception — prohibited under UKBA.

canonical_name: FCPA Accounting Provisions — Books, Records & Internal Controls (15 USC 78m)
description: FCPA Section 13(b): requires SEC issuers to (1) make and keep books, records, and accounts in reasonable detail that accurately and fairly reflect transactions and dispositions of assets (books and records provision); (2) devise and maintain a system of internal accounting controls sufficient to provide reasonable assurance that transactions are properly authorised and recorded. Applies regardless of whether bribery occurred — accounting failures alone can be prosecuted. Non-issuers are also subject to the DOJ's FCPA anti-bribery provisions.

Bribery is the offering, giving, receiving, or soliciting of a financial or other advantage to influence a person in their duties. Key elements vary by jurisdiction: UKBA focuses on 'improper performance of a function'; FCPA focuses on corrupt intent + business purpose. Active bribery = the offeror; passive bribery = the recipient. Bribery differs from corruption (broader) in that it requires a specific corrupt transaction. Extends beyond cash: includes gifts, hospitality, loans, job offers, political donations, facilitation payments.

Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain. UNCAC covers: bribery of national/foreign officials, trading in influence, embezzlement, misappropriation, abuse of functions, illicit enrichment, obstruction of justice, and money laundering of corruption proceeds. Bribery is the most commonly prosecuted form. Corruption is a predicate offence for money laundering under FATF R.3, AMLR Art.2, and most national AML laws — meaning proceeds of corruption are subject to AML/CFT controls.

A person who holds a legislative, administrative, or judicial position in a foreign country; or exercises a public function for a foreign country or a public international organisation; or is an official/agent of a public international organisation. FCPA and UKBA both use this concept but with subtle differences. State-owned enterprise (SOE) employees are typically treated as FPOs under FCPA and UKBA when they exercise government authority. PEPs overlap substantially with FPOs — high-risk in both ABC and AML contexts.

A public official exercising functions within their home country. UKBA s.1/s.2 cover bribery of domestic public officials (as well as private sector). FCPA does not cover bribery of domestic US officials — that falls under the US domestic bribery statute (18 USC 201). Under UNCAC, all state parties must criminalise domestic official bribery. Domestic PEPs in AML/ABC contexts require enhanced due diligence, particularly in high-risk jurisdictions.

Small unofficial payments to government officials to secure or expedite routine government services or actions to which the payer is already entitled (e.g., customs clearance, visa processing, utility connections). UKBA: no exception — facilitation payments are illegal under s.1 and s.6 regardless of amount or local custom. FCPA: narrow exception (15 USC 78dd-1(b)) for payments to secure 'routine governmental action' — but this exception is construed narrowly by DOJ/SEC and is increasingly disfavoured. Bona fide commercial best practice: zero-tolerance policy on facilitation payments.

Bona fide promotional or representational expenditure on gifts, meals, travel, accommodation, or entertainment for business partners, clients, or government officials. NOT inherently corrupt — but presents significant ABC risk when: excessive in value; provided to government officials or FPOs; tied to a pending decision; given repeatedly to the same person; not properly approved or recorded. ABC policies require prior approval for GHE above defined thresholds, maintenance of a gifts register, and zero tolerance for GHE to FPOs without legal review. UKBA and FCPA both treat GHE as potential bribery where corrupt intent is present.

A form of bribery where a portion of a payment received is secretly returned to the payer or another party. Common in procurement, construction, healthcare, and public contracts. Examples: contractor pays a percentage of contract value back to the procurement official who awarded it; pharmaceutical company pays undisclosed commissions to prescribing doctors. Kickbacks are a core typology in ABC investigations and are frequently also ML predicate offences.

The sole defence to the UKBA s.7 corporate offence. A commercial organisation must show it had in place 'adequate procedures designed to prevent persons associated with [it] from undertaking [bribery]'. The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) guidance sets out Six Principles for adequate procedures: (1) Proportionate procedures; (2) Top-level commitment; (3) Risk assessment; (4) Due diligence; (5) Communication (including training); (6) Monitoring and review. The standard is proportionality — procedures must be calibrated to the organisation's specific bribery risks. ISO 37001 certification is relevant evidence of adequate procedures.

canonical_name: Six Principles for Adequate Procedures (MoJ Guidance)
description: The Ministry of Justice guidance (2011) on 'adequate procedures' under UKBA s.7 establishes six principles: (1) Proportionate procedures — calibrated to bribery risk; (2) Top-level commitment — board-level tone at the top; (3) Risk assessment — periodic assessment of bribery risk across operations; (4) Due diligence — risk-based due diligence on associated persons; (5) Communication — training and communication of policies; (6) Monitoring and review — ongoing assessment of effectiveness. These principles underpin ISO 37001 and most major ABMS frameworks.

Risk-based due diligence on business associates (agents, consultants, intermediaries, joint venture partners, distributors) to assess and mitigate the risk that they might pay bribes on behalf of the organisation. The majority of FCPA and UKBA enforcement cases involve third-party bribery. Key indicators of third-party ABC risk: commission rates out of line with market; poor knowledge of the territory; government or political connections; requests for cash or payments to third countries; unwillingness to comply with ABC contractual terms. TPDD is a core component of adequate procedures under the Six Principles.

Third parties engaged to facilitate business, market access, or transactions on behalf of an organisation — including agents, consultants, distributors, local partners, joint venture partners, and brokers. The highest-risk category in ABC compliance. FCPA enforcement statistics: over 90% of enforcement actions involve third-party intermediaries. Intermediary ABC red flags: (1) No apparent legitimate business role; (2) Disproportionately high commission; (3) Government connections or FPO family members; (4) Requests for payments to third parties; (5) Location in high-corruption-risk jurisdiction; (6) Unwillingness to sign ABC representations. Contractual ABC provisions (representations, right to audit, termination on ABC breach) are a minimum requirement.

A situation where a person's private interests conflict with their professional duties, creating a risk of corruption or improper influence. ABC-relevant conflicts: an employee awarding a contract to a family member's company; a procurement official receiving stock options in a supplier; a government official on the board of a company they regulate. Conflicts of interest are a core ABC risk factor and a common predicate condition for bribery. Must be declared, assessed, and managed — typically via mandatory disclosure, recusal from decisions, or divestment.

Payments or donations to political parties, candidates, or political organisations. High ABC risk because: they may be made corruptly to influence government decisions; they can be disguised bribes in jurisdictions without strict campaign finance laws; state-owned enterprise employees may classify them as normal business expense. Many ABC policies prohibit or strictly limit political contributions. Must be distinguished from legitimate political engagement. FCPA and UKBA both cover corrupt political contributions where made to FPOs or to influence decisions.

Corporate sponsorships and charitable donations present ABC risk when they are: made at the suggestion of a government official or FPO; directed to organisations connected to officials; disproportionate to the legitimate business or reputational benefit; used to disguise improper payments. ABC compliance requires prior approval of sponsorships and donations above defined thresholds, assessment of connections to FPOs or government, and confirmation of bona fide charitable status. Many enforcement cases have involved 'charitable' payments that were in substance bribes.

canonical_name: ABC / Bribery Red Flags and Warning Indicators
description: Indicators that a bribery risk is present. Key red flags: (1) Agent requests unusually high commission or cash payment; (2) Agent has government connections or FPO family members; (3) Payment requested to an offshore account or different country; (4) Business won shortly after hiring a local agent; (5) Agent resists signing ABC contractual terms; (6) Hospitality requests from government official before a decision; (7) Invoice is vague or describes no services; (8) Unusual discounts to intermediaries; (9) Jurisdiction with high Transparency International CPI risk score; (10) Unusual accounting adjustments post-contract award. Must be assessed in third-party due diligence and ongoing monitoring.

A negotiated agreement between a prosecutor and a corporation in which the prosecutor agrees to defer (or drop) criminal charges in exchange for the organisation meeting specified conditions over a period (typically 2-5 years). UK DPAs: authorised under Crime and Courts Act 2013, approved by Crown Court, published. US DPAs: agreed with DOJ, increasingly used in FCPA cases. Conditions typically include: payment of a financial penalty, disgorgement of profits, appointment of an independent compliance monitor, cooperation with investigations, and implementation of enhanced compliance programme. DPAs have become the dominant resolution mechanism for corporate ABC enforcement in both the UK and US.

Proactive disclosure by a company to enforcement authorities (SFO, DOJ, SEC) of discovered bribery or ABC programme failures before investigation commences. Significant credit given for voluntary self-reporting under DOJ FCPA Corporate Enforcement Policy (CCP): companies that voluntarily self-disclose, fully cooperate, and remediate in good time are eligible for significant fine reductions (up to 50%) and may avoid criminal charges. SFO guidance similarly incentivises self-reporting. The self-reporting decision requires careful legal advice — disclosure triggers enhanced regulatory scrutiny and waives some privilege protections.

canonical_name: Books, Records & Internal Controls (FCPA Accounting Provisions)
description: The FCPA accounting provisions (15 USC 78m) require SEC issuers to: (1) maintain books and records that accurately reflect transactions; (2) maintain internal accounting controls providing reasonable assurance that transactions are properly authorised and recorded. These provisions are enforced independently of the anti-bribery provisions — companies have been prosecuted for books and records violations without evidence of actual bribery. Common books/records violations: off-books slush funds, undisclosed commission payments, mischaracterised entertainment expenses. Best practice: strong financial controls, expense pre-approval, and internal audit coverage of high-risk areas.

Bribery between private commercial parties, without involvement of a public official. Covered by UKBA s.1 and s.2 — there is no public official requirement. Private sector bribery examples: kickbacks in procurement; secret commissions to purchasing managers; undisclosed payments by a supplier to a customer's buyer. Less commonly prosecuted than public sector bribery but increasingly relevant in international supply chains. UNCAC Art.21 requires state parties to consider criminalising private sector bribery. EU Anti-Corruption Directive covers both public and private sector.

canonical_name: Grease Payments — FCPA Facilitating Payments Exception
description: Under the FCPA, a narrow exception exists for 'facilitating or expediting payments' to a foreign official to secure 'routine governmental action' (15 USC 78dd-1(b)). Routine governmental action: processing visas, providing police protection, scheduling inspections, providing utility services. The exception does NOT cover: obtaining or retaining contracts, influencing legislative or regulatory decisions. The DOJ/SEC construe this exception very narrowly and its use is strongly discouraged. Under the UKBA, there is NO equivalent exception — all facilitation payments are illegal regardless of amount or purpose.

Reduction in financial penalties or avoidance of criminal prosecution in exchange for substantial assistance with investigations. DOJ FCPA Corporate Enforcement Policy (2017, updated 2023): companies that voluntarily self-disclose, fully cooperate, and timely remediate are eligible for up to 50% reduction below the low end of the guidelines penalty range, and may avoid criminal resolution entirely in some cases. SFO cooperation: SFO guidance encourages self-reporting and offers significant credit for genuine co-operation. Relevant to individual executives: DOJ and SFO increasingly require companies to identify culpable individuals as a condition of corporate leniency.

The designated individual or team responsible for overseeing the organisation's anti-bribery and corruption compliance programme. Role covers: ABC risk assessment, policy development and maintenance, third-party due diligence oversight, training, gifts and hospitality approval, investigation management, and board reporting. ISO 37001 requires designation of an anti-bribery compliance function with appropriate authority and independence. In financial institutions, the ABC function typically sits within compliance, alongside or integrated with the AML/CFT function (as corruption is an AML predicate offence).

Periodic structured assessment of the organisation's exposure to bribery and corruption risk. Process: (1) Identify risk categories (geographic, sectoral, transactional, business partner, product/service, channel); (2) Assess inherent risk per category using risk indicators (CPI scores, government touch points, sector bribery typologies); (3) Assess existing controls (policies, training, TPDD, approvals); (4) Determine residual risk; (5) Identify mitigation actions; (6) Document and report to senior management/board. Must be reviewed periodically and on material change (new markets, mergers, new business lines). Feeds the Adequate Procedures defence under UKBA s.7.

Risk-based process for assessing business associates before engagement and on an ongoing basis. Tiers: (1) Light-touch screening (low-risk, commodity suppliers) — name screening, public record check; (2) Standard DD (medium-risk) — company verification, beneficial ownership, CPI screening, ABC questionnaire; (3) Enhanced DD (high-risk: government-facing agents, high-risk jurisdictions, large commissions) — background investigation, reference checks, site visit, senior approval. Key outputs: risk rating, approval or rejection, contractual ABC clauses, ongoing monitoring schedule. Major FCPA/UKBA failures have involved inadequate TPDD of agents paying bribes.

canonical_name: Gifts & Hospitality Approval and Recording Process
description: Process governing the giving and receiving of gifts, hospitality, and entertainment. Key elements: (1) Pre-approval requirement for GHE above defined monetary thresholds (typically lower thresholds for government officials/FPOs, or zero tolerance); (2) Gifts register — log of all GHE given and received; (3) Annual review of register for patterns; (4) Prohibition on cash gifts; (5) Policy on meals and entertainment (reasonable, proportionate, documented); (6) Travel/accommodation policy (commercial rates, not personal); (7) Explicit prohibition on GHE to FPOs without legal advice and senior approval. GHE is one of the most common entry points for bribery in practice.

Mechanism for employees, agents, and third parties to report suspected bribery or ABC policy violations, including anonymously. Key elements: (1) Multiple reporting channels (hotline, web portal, line manager, compliance officer, audit committee); (2) Anonymous and confidential reporting options; (3) Non-retaliation policy (protected disclosure); (4) Investigation of all substantive reports; (5) Feedback to reporters (where possible); (6) Escalation to senior management/audit committee for material concerns; (7) External reporting mechanism (to SFO, DOJ) if self-reporting is warranted. Speak-up programmes are a core component of the Six Principles (communication and monitoring). ISO 37001 requires a reporting mechanism.

Structured investigation process when a bribery allegation or red flag is identified. Phases: (1) Triage — assess allegation seriousness and determine investigation scope; (2) Preservation — secure relevant documents and data (legal hold); (3) Investigation — interviews, document review, forensic accounting, digital forensics; (4) Findings — assess evidence against legal standard; (5) Remediation — disciplinary action, process improvements, compensation where required; (6) Self-reporting decision — legal advice on whether regulatory disclosure is required or warranted. Privilege: internal investigation reports may attract legal professional privilege — requires careful privilege structuring from the outset.

Mandatory anti-bribery and corruption training for all staff and relevant third parties. Key elements: (1) General awareness training for all staff (what bribery is, how to identify it, how to report it); (2) Role-specific training for high-risk roles (sales, procurement, government affairs, finance, legal); (3) Board and senior management training; (4) Training records — completion tracking and certification; (5) Periodic refresher training (typically annual); (6) Training for agents and intermediaries on the organisation's ABC standards; (7) Real-world case studies and red flag recognition exercises. Training is one of the Six Principles and a core ISO 37001 requirement.

UK government department and law enforcement agency responsible for investigating and prosecuting serious or complex fraud, bribery, and corruption. Enforces the UK Bribery Act 2010 for corporate and individual offences. Powers include: s.2 CJSA 1987 compulsory production of documents, search warrants, international mutual legal assistance. Has concluded significant DPAs (Rolls-Royce 2017, Airbus 2020, G4S 2020, Serco 2021). Director appointed by Attorney General. Subject to judicial oversight for DPAs (must be in interests of justice and fair, reasonable, proportionate terms).

canonical_name: US Department of Justice — FCPA Enforcement (Criminal Division)
description: The Fraud Section of the DOJ Criminal Division is the primary enforcer of the FCPA's anti-bribery provisions. Pursues both corporate (DPA/NPA/plea agreement) and individual (criminal prosecution) enforcement. DOJ FCPA Corporate Enforcement Policy (2017, updated 2022/2023) sets out cooperation incentives. Maintains the FCPA Resource Guide (with SEC) as the principal interpretive document. Has pursued enforcement globally — Siemens ($800M, 2008), Odebrecht ($2.6bn, 2016), Goldman Sachs 1MDB ($2.9bn, 2020). Coordinates with SFO, OFAC, and foreign authorities.

canonical_name: US Securities and Exchange Commission — FCPA Enforcement
description: The SEC enforces the FCPA's accounting provisions (books and records, internal controls) against SEC issuers and their officers/directors. Brings civil enforcement actions — disgorgement of profits, civil monetary penalties, officer/director bars. Coordinates with DOJ on parallel criminal/civil proceedings. The SEC's Enforcement Division has a dedicated FCPA unit. Non-US issuers listed in the US (ADR holders) are subject to SEC FCPA jurisdiction. The SEC jointly publishes the FCPA Resource Guide with DOJ.

The monitoring body for the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention. Conducts Phase 1-4 peer reviews of all 44 signatory countries assessing: legislative implementation of the Convention, enforcement track record, awareness campaigns, and emerging issues. Phase 4 evaluations (2017 onwards) focus heavily on enforcement effectiveness. OECD WGB recommendations are influential — persistent failures can trigger formal follow-up and reputational pressure. The WGB has noted under-enforcement by several EU member states. Publishes annual enforcement data.

canonical_name: UNODC — UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNCAC Secretariat)
description: The secretariat for the UN Convention Against Corruption (UNCAC) and its Implementation Review Mechanism (IRM). UNODC provides technical assistance to state parties on anti-corruption law and policy, supports the UNCAC Review Mechanism peer reviews, and publishes reports on corruption trends and good practices. The UNODC also administers the UN Global Programme against Corruption (GPAC) and supports anti-corruption courts and institutions in developing countries.

EU body established in 2021 with the power to investigate and prosecute criminal offences affecting the EU's financial interests (PIF Directive). Covers: fraud against EU funds, VAT fraud exceeding EUR 10M, and corruption affecting EU financial interests. EPPO operates in 22 EU member states (not Hungary, Poland, Sweden, or Ireland). Can pursue cross-border criminal investigations across member states using a unified legal framework. The EU Anti-Corruption Directive (proposed 2023) would extend EPPO's coordination role.

The EU anti-fraud body responsible for investigating fraud, corruption, and other financial irregularities affecting the EU budget. OLAF conducts administrative investigations and refers criminal matters to national authorities or EPPO. Jurisdiction: EU institutions, agencies, and bodies; EU-funded programmes in member states and third countries. OLAF's investigations result in recommendations to national authorities for prosecution, recovery of funds, or disciplinary action. Does not have its own criminal prosecution power — relies on national prosecutors.

canonical_name: GRECO — Group of States Against Corruption (Council of Europe)
description: Council of Europe monitoring body for anti-corruption standards. GRECO evaluates compliance with: Council of Europe Criminal Law Convention on Corruption (ETS 173), Civil Law Convention on Corruption (ETS 174), and additional CoE standards. 49 member states including all EU members and the US/UK. Evaluation themes: incrimination, transparency of party funding, integrity of parliamentarians/judges/prosecutors/law enforcement, and conflict of interest. GRECO recommendations are non-binding but politically significant.

canonical_name: ABC × AMLR — Bribery as Money Laundering Predicate Offence
description: Under AMLR 2024/1624, corruption and bribery are predicate offences for money laundering — proceeds of bribery are subject to AML/CFT controls. AMLR Art.2 incorporates the predicate offence list from AMLD6/Palermo Convention, which includes corruption, bribery, and fraud against financial interests. This means: financial institutions must identify and report bribery-related suspicions via SAR/STR; PEPs screening is both an AML and ABC control; third-party corruption proceeds flowing through accounts trigger transaction monitoring alerts. The ABC and AML compliance functions must be coordinated — typically the MLRO and anti-corruption officer should communicate on overlapping cases.

canonical_name: ABC × FATF — Corruption as ML Predicate (FATF R.3)
description: FATF Recommendation 3 requires countries to criminalise money laundering for the widest possible range of predicate offences, explicitly including corruption (FATF R.3 glossary). The FATF Methodology (Immediate Outcome 1 and 7) assesses whether ML from corruption proceeds is effectively investigated and prosecuted. FATF mutual evaluations regularly cite inadequate investigation of corruption-related ML as an effectiveness gap. The FATF and Egmont Group have published typology reports on ML from corruption and kleptocracy. FATF's guidance on PEP risk (Recommendation 12) is directly relevant to ABC third-party screening.

CSRD (Directive 2022/2464) requires large undertakings to report sustainability information including governance matters. ESRS G1 (Business Conduct) requires disclosure of: anti-corruption policies and procedures; training; incidents and confirmed cases of corruption/bribery; legal proceedings for corruption. Companies must disclose material governance risks including ABC risk exposure. SFDR PAI indicators include conviction of corruption/bribery as a principal adverse impact indicator. Investors and ESG rating agencies increasingly assess ABC programme quality as part of governance scoring.

canonical_name: ABC × Sanctions — State-Linked Corruption and FPO Overlap
description: Significant overlap between ABC compliance and sanctions: (1) FPOs and PEPs sanctioned by OFAC, OFSI, or EU for corruption (e.g., under US Global Magnitsky Act, EU Global Human Rights Sanctions Regime) are subject to both ABC due diligence and sanctions controls; (2) Bribery of officials of sanctioned states (e.g., Russia, Iran) may simultaneously violate ABC laws and sanctions prohibitions; (3) Corruption proceeds may flow through sanctioned jurisdictions or entities. ABC and sanctions teams must coordinate — particularly for third-party due diligence where government-connected parties may appear on both ABC watchlists and sanctions lists.

canonical_name: UK Bribery Act / FCPA × UNCAC Alignment
description: Both the UKBA and FCPA are considered broadly consistent with UNCAC obligations, though UNCAC has a broader scope. UNCAC Art.16 (bribery of foreign officials) aligns with UKBA s.6 and FCPA. UNCAC Art.21 (private sector bribery) aligns with UKBA s.1/s.2 but has no FCPA equivalent. UNCAC Art.14 (money laundering measures) overlaps with AML/CFT obligations applicable to bribery proceeds. UNCAC Art.52-57 (asset recovery) underpin international cooperation in ABC enforcement and are referenced in SFO's international mutual legal assistance requests.

Key differences between UKBA and FCPA: (1) Facilitation payments: FCPA narrow exception; UKBA absolute prohibition. (2) Private sector: UKBA covers B2B bribery (s.1/s.2); FCPA covers only FPO bribery. (3) Corporate liability: UKBA s.7 strict liability (intent irrelevant); FCPA requires corrupt intent. (4) Territorial reach: both extraterritorial but UKBA is broader — any commercial organisation with a UK nexus. (5) Hospitality: FCPA permits bona fide promotional expenses; UKBA requires no corrupt intent. (6) Enforcement: FCPA — DOJ (criminal) + SEC (civil); UKBA — SFO only. Understanding both frameworks is essential for multinational companies with UK and US operations.

canonical_name: ABC × Criminal Law — Investigation and Prosecution Interface
description: ABC corporate compliance intersects with criminal law at several points: (1) Internal investigations — results may be used as evidence in criminal proceedings; privilege must be protected from the outset; (2) DPA negotiations — criminal charges deferred in exchange for cooperation and compliance; (3) Individual prosecution — DOJ/SFO increasingly pursue individuals alongside corporates; (4) Dawn raids — search and seizure powers can compel production of ABC investigation records; (5) Mutual Legal Assistance — cross-border evidence sharing (MLA treaties, European Investigation Order); (6) Whistleblower protection — criminal sanctions for retaliation against whistleblowers in some jurisdictions.
